Title/Name: Aird guides at the Giant's Causeway
Description: As more and more visitors began to travel to the Giant's Causeway from the 18th century, a local tourism industry began to develop. Local people would take tourists to the famous Causeway stones and coastline, regaling them with tales and facts about the area. These photographs show local guides from the Causeway in the early 20th century. Photo 1 shows Edwardian visitors pictured with guides in front of the old Causeway School building, what is now the Nook restaurant. This is almost certainly an 'excursion' of, rather well attired, visitors possibly taken to the Causeway on the horse-drawn cart from somewhere like Portrush or another local holiday resort. Photo 2 depicts local guides from the Aird. Submitter Brian Bolt remembers these guides from his childhood: (back) Robert Colvin, Jamie McMullan, John Colvin and (front) Johnny Martin and Johnny McLernon. Photo 3: Johnny McLernon and Joe Mornin. These men, like many Causeway guides, were fishermen who routinely carried baskets of fish up from the steep bays of the Causeway Coast and who were able to work as guides to supplement their income.

Title/Name: An Emperor's secret visit to the Giant's Causeway
Description:
The article below was developed using research and images kindly submitted by local submitter John Logan. There are few who know of Brazilian Emperor Dom Pedro’s unofficial visit to Ireland in 1877.

Dom Pedro was a ‘super-tourist’ of his time, a frequent traveller who was referred to by some in his home country as ‘Pedro da Mala’ (Pedro of the suitcase!). An educated and academically minded man, Dom Pedro had a keen interest in history and science and was a great lover of geology in particular.

Hence, there was one spot that the Brazilian Emperor made sure to visit during his trip to Ireland – the Giants Causeway. Even in the 19th century the Giants Causeway and spectacular Causeway Coast were renowned for their outstanding world-class geology.On Monday 9th July 1877, Dom Pedro and his entourage arrived in Belfast on the SS Antrim, where they were greeted by a small delegation. The Emperor’s trip was not publicised and details were to be kept largely private. It is likely that the secretive nature of the visit was due to the fact that Dom Pedro was accompanied on the trip by not only his wife, but also his suspected lover- the Countess of Barral.

After arriving in Belfast, the Royal Party travelled to the Causeway Coast in the first-class carriages of the Belfast and Northern Counties Railway. The train was bedecked at the front with crossed Union and Brazilian Flags to mark the occasion. Once the train arrived at Portrush, Dom Pedro and his party were escorted straight to the Giants Causeway from the station via carriage.Once at the Causeway, the distinguished guests found themselves at Mr Francis Kane’s little hotel at Causeway Head where the Emperor enjoyed a cup of coffee presented by Mrs Kane, before being led by guides down to inspect the Causeway Stones. Once there, Dom Pedro walked as far as the Lord Antrim’s Parlour admiring the impressive geological formations before him. Eventually he met the photographer Mr Daniel McKinlay who requested that he sit for a photograph at the Stones. The Emperor happily agreed and later Mr McKinlay received a request for 100 copies of the photograph from Dom Pedro’s personal secretary. At the conclusion of their visit the Royal Party purchased souvenirs, including rock specimens, from vendors along the coast before heading back to Portrush train station. Here word had spread and many locals crowded the station to get a glimpse of the Emperor and Empress, giving the Royals a warm send off and cheering as their train departed!

Like innumerable visitors before and since, Dom Pedro is noted to have thoroughly enjoyed his visit to the Giants Causeway. Now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Giants Causeway and Causeway Coast continues to attract visitors from across the globe, almost 150 years after this unusual footnote in the area’s long and rich history.

Description: Ballintoy Archaeological and Historical Society was established in 2010 to promote awareness of, and encourage research into, the rich history and heritage of Ballintoy and the surrounding district. The Society meets on the last Thursday of each month (except December, July and August) in Ballintoy Parish Hall at 8pm. The Society's email address is bahs@live.co.uk.

Situated near the shore, Ballintoy Parish Church is arguably the most painted and photographed church in Northern Ireland and it is visited by people from throughout the world.

There has been a church on this site since the early seventeenth century, but the present building was erected in 1813 during the incumbency of the Rev. Robert Traill. The new church, which cost £1324 11s 6 ½d, was inspected by three commissioners for the Bishop of Down and Connor and on 1 April 1814 they advised the Bishop that ‘the roof well timbered and slated with the best ton slates...the seats commodious...all neatly finished and painted...the church is neat, the steeple handsome and well-executed.’

The new church, particularly its steeple, stood out in an impressive but barren landscape. In the Parliamentary Gazetteer of Ireland published in 1844 the steeple was described as ‘a conspicuous object in so bleak a view, and has become a useful landmark to mariners.’ It consisted of a tower, which may have been part of the previous church, a slated spire, composed of wood and plaster, topped with a weather vane. Unfortunately the spire was blown away, together with part of the church’s roof, in a gale early on the morning of Saturday 22 December 1894. The roof was repaired, but sadly the spire was not rebuilt. Nonetheless, the church remains an iconic landmark on the north Antrim coast.

Image courtesy of National Library of Ireland.

Up near Ballintoy, Charlie Witherspoon visits an unusual house built by a mysterious man who declined to be interviewed or filmed. The house is still under construction and had been now for 29 years. It’s a maze of rooms with no apparent plan. The internal artwork is staggering. Now we do know the story of Bendhu House and its original owner thanks to research including the book, Bendhu and its Builders by Andrew Cowser. ‘Bendhu was the creation of Newton Penprase, a remarkable Cornish artist based in Belfast,’ explains Cowser, an architecture lecturer at Queen's University.

Description:
Footage of an employee at Bushmill's Distillery showing the various processes to make a cooper.

Before long, the cooper "gets rolled down to the tester who puts a bit of water in it". Once this test is passed, the cooper is ready for alcohol to be stored in it. Also features shots of the distillery itself.

These photographs were kindly submitted to the Uncharted Histories Project by Frank Scott. They show 'Aky' Walker, chauffeur to Mrs Denny of Ballylough House. Mrs Denny was a member of the Traill family and established a cottage industry at Castlecatt in the early 20th century which provided employment for local people.

People from the area worked together at The Basket House, Castlecatt to produce baskets and other crafts for sale across the area. Mrs Denny even sent apprentices to England to learn new skills and bring them back to the Causeway Coast. These photographs are held by Mrs Sarah Scott, Frank’s wife. They were taken in the 1920s or 1930s and came to her from her older sister, Elizabeth Grey (née Walker). Elizabeth and another of Sarah’s older sisters worked for Mrs Denny, as did their father Aky Walker.

Local man Brian Bolt shared a collection of school photographs from his time at the Causeway Memorial School in the 1950s. Brian remembers his time at the school fondly and remembers his schoolmates well. The Causeway School was built in 1915 by Lord McNaghtan of Runkerry, replacing a previous school which had been situated at what is now the Nook restaurant. The school building was designed by eminent architect Clough Williams-Ellis, who is famous for designing and building the unique village of Portmeirion, Wales. The Causeway School was closed in 1962 and later became a Museum visited by many schoolchildren in the Causeway Coast and Glens area until 2013. In 2019 the School was transferred into the ownership of the National Trust for restoration.

A paupers’ graveyard created in the 19th century by the Ballycastle Guardians.

Around 400 paupers who died in Ballycastle Workhouse are buried here, as well as, according to Danny Morgan, the remains of a German Princess, who died while visiting the area as part of a traveling circus. The spelling and origin of the placename is not agreed, with some people calling it 'Crocknakinney'. The first element comes from the Irish 'cnoc' for a hill, but the second could be from 'tsionnaigh' < 'sionnach' (fox) or 'connaidh' < 'connadh' (firewood), or, it is plausible that 'tine' for fire is in place, but in all these cases grammatically the name should render as 'Cnocknatinney'. There has been a suggestion that this site was previously used as a the location for a signal fire, but it may also simply have served as a valuable source of firewood in a coastal area where trees are typically sparse.

Title/Name: Embankment of the Coast Road at Altrahack, Ballintoy Demesne
Description: The Irish word ‘alt’ refers to a glen or ravine with a river running through it. When the coast road was built it had to be supported by this embankment to cross the ravine. It is said locally that a man called Culvin Getty was murdered here by hanging him over the top of the wall by his hair before cutting his Achilles tendons and dropping him to the ground below. He supposedly managed to crawl from here to the cliff edge before falling into the sea.

In this footage we see visitors enjoying many of the entertainments it has to offer, be it the miniature train and Moon Rocket at Barry's Amusements, a frolic in the paddling pool, or donkey ride on one of the pristine beaches.

Remains of one of many kelp kilns still to be found along the Causeway Coast.

The manufacture of kelp in Ireland from the 17th to early 20th centuries provided soda and later iodine for contemporary industries. It was an immensely important element of coastal economies, and notably for island communities, often impoverished and with limited agricultural means.

Click here for kelp industry article by local archaeologist Wes Forsythe.

This is a stone-lined rectangular kelp kiln located near the causeway footpath of Dunseverick Harbour. The kiln is a survival of the kelp industry active in North Antrim from 18th-19th centuries. It is one of the few North Antrim kiln sites to survive, and is a particularly good example, being almost intact. Kelp was used to make soda and iodine for industry.

Description: Locally known as 'The Cups and Saucers', Lissanduff earthworks are large ancient monuments located just outside the coastal village of Portballintrae. This fine example of ancient earthworks (potentially dating to the Iron Age, c.500BC) consists of large circular enclosures. The precise function of these structures is unknown. One of the earthworks is located over a natural spring, and it is believed that they may have had some ritual or spiritual purpose. This site is a scheduled monument and is publicly accessible to the public.

Many have seen the imposing spectacle of Long Gilbert Quarry when driving along the spectacular Dunluce Road between Portrush and Bushmills. Many a car passenger may have gazed into the cavern of the quarry when driving past, but most don't know of its history. For hundreds of years limestone was quarried at this location - the two large buildings still visible are the remains of huge lime kilns where limestone was burned to produce quicklime. Quicklime was used in agriculture and construction, and is now used in steelmaking, glass works and many other industries. The site's name is said to have come from a tall gangly jester for a Lord of Antrim, nicknamed 'Long Gilbert'. Title/Name: Maghernahar artefacts uncovered through field walking
Description:
These items were uncovered by the McGill family in the agricultural fields surrounding their home, through years of field walking. While walking through freshly ploughed fields, a selection of stone age artefacts were found which include small flint tools from the era of Ireland's first settlers.

These Mesolithic 'microliths' are tiny stone tools made c.8,000 to 10,000 years ago. Later neolithic (c.4,000-6,000 years old) stone tools including large 'Bann flakes', scrapers, awls and other miscellaneous items are also found in the McGill collection. A fragment of a porcellanite polished axe head was uncovered, this unique stone was traded by neolotihic peoples in North Antrim and was mined only in two locations at Tievebulliagh, Cushendall and on Rathlin island.

Later artefacts include clay pipes, which show the 'red hand of Ulster' stamp found commonly on Ulster pipes in the 19th century.

Description:
The Causeway Coast and wider landscape is home to numerous ruins of small cottages and homesteads. Many notice the remains of these small homes from days gone by as you travel the countryside, where families lived and worked. Often the stories and connections for these homesteads are lost. However, this example is the remains of the McDade homestead at Carnsampson.

Family history researcher, Sean T. Traynor submitted the following information: 'This is my grandmother's family homestead, the McDade's of Carnsampson, with the wall still standing. My Dad and all his siblings were born here, as was my grandmother in 1909'. Sean's great great great grandfather James McDaid is first listed as renting the land in 1861.

Description:
Mrs Craig lived with her husband behind the Masonic Hall in Moyarget, on a road known as McGowan's Brae (she was one of six McGowan sisters).

Moyarget is the name of an ancient silvermine, as its name might suggest (airgeadmeaning 'silver' in Irish). The other five McGowan sisters married men named McCaughan, Hill, McPherson, McGowan and McGowan (no relations). There was no brother to inherit the McGowan family farm, so a family named Hill got it - perhaps the Hills into whose family one McGowan sister married.

Title/Name: Old lazy beds below Lannimore Hill, Black Park, Ballintoy Demesne
Description: These lazy beds lie in a field belonging to Maurice McHenry. Maurice's father bought the farm in the 1930s, and Maurice inherited it from him in 1970. The McHenrys are sheep farmers, and Maurice does not remember the lazy beds being used in his lifetime. He was told that barley and oats were probably the last crop to be planted there. Sheep farming was introduced to the area by the local landowners, the Stewart family, in the era of Improvement.

Title/Name: Orange Hall, formerly a school, Ballintoy Demesne
Description: The Orange Hall at Ballintoy Demesne was previously a school, established by the Fullerton family. It is now a listed building and the property includes two beautiful examples of traditional stone gateposts.

Starting in the 1830s Port Moon was a centre of salmon fishing. Nets were stretched out between rocks to catch salmon migrating across the Atlantic to spawn in the River Bush. The fisherman's bothy has been restored and is used as a stopover for kayakers exploring the Causeway Coast.

Description:
On Portrush's East Strand a WWII 'pill box' can be seen, set into the wall of a private residence. This is one of two defences constructed in Portrush after 1940.

Pill boxes were defences constructed around the coast by the UK government during the war. These small fortifications were built to provide shelter for troops and artillery, and were designed to help defend the coast in the event of a German invasion. See Portrush Heritage Group Newsletter Issue 4 by Francis Wilson for more information. Portrush Heritage Group is a charitable heritage group run by community volunteers in the Portrush area. This group seeks to explore and share the heritage of Portrush and the North Antrim coast.

Visit discoverportrush.com to learn more about the work of the group and to explore their many resources and projects. You can also download the free Discover Portrush Trail App, which offers a digital tour of the town.

The railway first came to Portrush in 1855, with the completion of the Ballymena, Ballymoney, Coleraine and Portrush Junction Railway. The arrival of the railway helped Portrush flourish into a sea side resort, with many daytrippers and visitors travelling there to enjoy the stunning Causeway Coast. So successful was the railway that a new train station was needed to cope with the volume of traffic. In 1888 a new station was built by the Belfast and Northern Counties railway, designed by famous civil engineer Berkeley Deane Wise. Information courtesy of Portrush Heritage Group. This ruined barn once operated as a soup kitchen which may have been run by the Christies, who were successful large farmers in the area. The Christies, who ran the soup kitchen, were relatives of Sean McKinley. His mother was a Christie and was raised in a two-storey farm house on the opposite side of the road from the soup kitchen. Barney Christie (an uncle?) went to America to work as a lumberjack and sent money home to his father and Uncle Alec to save for him. He hoped to buy a farm with it when he returned, but came home to find that they had spent it all. He fell on hard times and tried to make a living trading horses, but was seen in church with holes in his trousers and eventually ended up locked up in a home at Tobernavine (?). When he eventually died, Sean McKinley’s father bought a portion of the Christie’s farm.

A poem by James McAllister of Bushmills

There is a small village not far from my home;
In the days of my youth there I oft times did roam
To speak of a hero known many miles around;
A champion oarsman his name is ‘Joe Brown’
Now this here I mention and his name I tell to you;
With the three ‘Curry Brothers’ made up that boat crew
Being oarsmen of valour they proved honour soon,
It was these famous four that belonged to Portmoon
The course being selected lay near Ramore Hill,
Where the boys of Portmoon met the men from Moville
In their fast racing drontheim called “Arrow” by name
Her crew and her coxswain – five heros of fame
They came from Moville and from sweet Innishown;
To be beaten by any it never was known
But their glorious honour that day was pulled down;
By the three ‘Curry Brothers’ and famed ‘Joe Brown’
As they lay there awaiting the start;
‘James Martin’ the coxswain, brought joy to their hearts,
For he says “my brave men” with a smile on his face,
“I’ll steer you to victory and win this great race”
‘Jackson Mill’ from Portmoon when this great race was ore,
Met these champion heros from Lochaber shore
Says “your victory this day proves your valour to all
From Fair Head in Antrim to famed Donegal”
Now to conclude and to finish my song;
I now leave it to others to correct where I’m wrong,
Near the famed “Giant’s Causeway” in a quiet humble home
You will there find the author of this little poem

This poem was submitted to the Uncharted Histories project by Maurice McCurdy

Title/Name: The Death of a Viking King
Description:
Close to the fourth hole on Royal Portrush's Valley links, is a spot named 'The War Hollow'. It is here where it is rumoured that King Magnus Barefoot of Norway met his end in an ambush by the Irish in 1103AD. It is claimed that the Norse King was anchored off the Skerries and went ashore to find a raiding party he had sent in search of cattle. Historical sources confirm that The King was killed somewhere in Ulster and was buried close to the Northern Irish coast. These men, including the Gault brothers, Dan McClelland and James Wilkinson, worked hard to fish along the Causeway Coast. Description:
It is October 1588 and the Spanish Galleass Girona has survived fire, ships in the English Channel and storms as it retreats north, round Scotland and down the west coast of Ireland. Seven hundred survivors, mainly from the nobility from the Encoranada and other ships, join the Girona setting sail from Killybegs along the treacherous north coast of Ireland to Catholic Scotland heading straight into another violent storm.

The ship built for 500 crew was now carrying 1300 people. At the same time a small community living on the north coast is about to witness the most extraordinary event in their lives. Father O'Connell is meeting with the local chief, Sorley Boy MacDonell, at Dunluce Castle to discuss the alarming news of the fleet of Spanish warships. Betsie, who works in the kitchens, overhears their conversation. Later that evening the Girona was off Lacada Point and was in imminent danger. As the ship comes too close to the shore, Betsie is horrified by what she sees.

This recording is an extract of a play written by Geraldine Fitzgerald called 'The Girona', read by Teresa Godfrey. Photo by Richard Sloan.

Description:
The growth of railway networks supported a thriving Tourism industry along the Causeway Coast in the later 19th century. The mainline railway to Portrush had been completed in the 1850s, and in the 1880s a cutting edge project would extend transport links from Portrush directly to the popular Giant's Causeway.

Local engineer William Acheson Traill pioneered the use of electrical traction for the construction of a roadside tramway from Portrush to Bushmills by 1883, later extended to the Giant's Causeway in 1887. This tramway was the world's first hydroelectric tramway, and was powered by a hydro-electric power station at Walkmills, Bushmills.

The tramway operated for over 60 years, closing in 1949. In its heyday it transported thousands of early tourists to the Causeway and Bushmills, as depicted in these photographs submitted by Maurice McCurdy of Lisnagunague.

Remnants of the tramway can still be seen along its old route and in recent years a section from Bushmills to the Causeway has been converted into a narrow gauge railway which can still be enjoyed by visitors.

Images courtesy of Maurice McCurdy.

Description:
This photograph shows Portrush Harbourmaster William Mann (c.1836-1904) in the late 19th century. This old family photo was submitted by Norman Parkes and shows his great gandfather William seated in front of a boat being launched at the harbour's beach. The boat was named the 'Caravogue’.

This photo was originally uncovered in the records of one of William Mann's descendants, who had emigrated to the USA in the early 1900s. The lady seated beside William is his wife, Mary Rafferty of Coleraine.
